pages.text:
M-68. A Double-Blind, Placebo-Cotrolled Study of
Rituximab in Patients with Stiff-Person Syndrome
(SPS)
Marinos C. Dalakas, Goran Rakocevic, James Dambrosia,
and Beverly McElroy; London, United Kingdom;
Philadelphia, PA and Bethesda, MD
In SPS, anti-GAD antibodies seem to affect GABAergic neu-
rotransmission resulting in stiffness and spasms. Most pa-
tients respond to GABA-enhancing drugs and IVIg (based
on a controlled study), but several remain disabled. The need
for more effective therapy prompted a trial with Rituximab,
a B cell-depleting agent. 24 patients were randomized to pla-
cebo or Rituximab (two biweekly infusions of 1 gram each).
The primary outcome was a change in stiffness and
heightened-sensitivity scores using validated scales (Dalakas
et al NEJM 2001). Enrolling 24 patients was calculated to
detect 50% change in scores (0.83 variance; power 0.80;
type-I error 0.05). Randomization was balanced for age, sex,
disease duration and GAD titers. No significant treatment
differences between the two groups were noted at 3 or 6
months in all scores. Significant (p /H110210.01) improvements
were however noted at 3 months for both treatment groups,
including QoL scores, indicating a strong placebo effect.
GAD antibody titers fluctuated upwards in both groups after
treatments. In spite of the overall negative study, presumably
because of strong placebo responses, 4 patients had definite
improvement after Rituximab based on clinical and video-
tape analysis of function.
